source: Jehle & Reny — Ch09 Auctions Mechanism Part2

items.statement: For all incentive-compatible direct selling mechanisms p_i(·), c_i(·), the seller's revenue satisfies R ≤ ∫₀¹···∫₀¹ Σᵢ p*_i(v₁,...,vₙ) [vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ)] f₁(v₁)···fₙ(vₙ) dv₁···dvₙ, where the upper bound is obtained by setting each c̄ᵢ(0) = 0 (since constraint (iii) implies c̄ᵢ(0) ≤ 0).
items.proof_sketch: Because constraint (iii) implies that each c̄ᵢ(0) ≤ 0, the revenue expression from (9.11) is bounded above by setting c̄ᵢ(0) = 0.
items.context: This is equation (9.14), establishing the revenue upper bound for any incentive-compatible direct selling mechanism.

notation_in_scope.Fᵢ: CDF of bidder i's value distribution
notation_in_scope.fᵢ: PDF of bidder i's value distribution
notation_in_scope.c̄ᵢ(0): expected cost to bidder i when his value is 0

items.statement: Define cost functions c*_i(v₁,...,vₙ) = c*_i(0,v₋ᵢ) + p*_i(v₁,...,vₙ)vᵢ - ∫₀^{vᵢ} p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ)dx. If the relationship between averages c̄*_i and p̄*_i required by constraint (ii) holds for each vector of values, then it holds for the averages. Setting c*_i(0,v₋ᵢ) = 0 for all i satisfies constraint (iii).
items.proof_sketch: Because c̄*_i and p̄*_i are averages of c*_i and p*_i, the required relationship between averages will hold if it holds for each and every vector of values v₁,...,vₙ.
items.context: Construction of optimal cost functions (equations 9.15 and 9.17) for the revenue-maximizing mechanism.

notation_in_scope.c*_i: optimal cost function for bidder i
notation_in_scope.v₋ᵢ: vector of all bidders' values except bidder i

items.statement: The candidate optimal mechanism defined by (9.16) and (9.17) satisfies constraints (ii) and (iii) by construction, and achieves the revenue upper bound in (9.14). The seller's revenues equal R = ∫₀¹···∫₀¹ Σᵢ p*_i(v₁,...,vₙ)[vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ)] f₁(v₁)···fₙ(vₙ) dv₁···dvₙ, their maximum possible value.
items.proof_sketch: Substitute the p*_i into (9.11) and recall that by construction c̄*_i(0) = 0 for every i.
items.context: Verification that the constructed mechanism achieves the revenue upper bound.

items.statement: The regularity condition (or monotone virtual value condition): For every i = 1,...,N, the virtual valuation vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is strictly increasing in vᵢ.
items.context: This is assumption (9.18), required to ensure that the optimal probability assignment functions satisfy constraint (i).

notation_in_scope.Fᵢ: CDF of bidder i's value distribution
notation_in_scope.fᵢ: PDF of bidder i's value distribution

items.statement: Assumption (9.18) is satisfied whenever each Fᵢ is any convex function, including the uniform distribution.
items.context: Stated as a fact that the reader is asked to verify in an exercise.

notation_in_scope.Fᵢ: CDF of bidder i's value distribution

items.statement: Under assumption (9.18), the virtual valuations v₁ - (1-F₁(v₁))/f₁(v₁), ..., vₙ - (1-Fₙ(vₙ))/fₙ(vₙ) are distinct with probability one.
items.proof_sketch: The strictly increasing transformation of independent continuous random variables produces values that are distinct with probability one.
items.context: This justifies the earlier assumption that the bracketed terms are distinct with probability one.

items.statement: Under assumption (9.18), if p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1 and v̄ᵢ > vᵢ, then p*_i(v̄ᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1. Consequently, p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) is non-decreasing in vᵢ for every v₋ᵢ, and therefore p̄*_i(vᵢ) is non-decreasing in vᵢ, so constraint (i) is satisfied.
items.proof: Consider some bidder i and some fixed vector of values v₋ᵢ for the other bidders. Suppose that v̄ᵢ > vᵢ and that p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1. Then by definition of p*_i, vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is positive and strictly greater than vⱼ - (1-Fⱼ(vⱼ))/fⱼ(vⱼ) for all j ≠ i. Because vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is strictly increasing (by (9.18)), v̄ᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(v̄ᵢ))/fᵢ(v̄ᵢ) is both positive and strictly greater than vⱼ - (1-Fⱼ(vⱼ))/fⱼ(vⱼ) for all j ≠ i, which means p*_i(v̄ᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1. Because p*_i takes values 0 or 1, p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) is non-decreasing in vᵢ for every v₋ᵢ. This implies p̄*_i(vᵢ) is non-decreasing in vᵢ.
items.context: This establishes that under the regularity condition, the constructed mechanism satisfies the monotonicity constraint (i).

items.statement: If N bidders have independent private values with bidder i's value drawn from the continuous positive density fᵢ satisfying (9.18) (i.e., vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is strictly increasing in vᵢ for every i), then the direct selling mechanism defined by (9.16) (p*_i assigns the object to the bidder with highest positive virtual valuation) and (9.17) (c*_i(v₁,...,vₙ) = p*_i(v₁,...,vₙ)vᵢ - ∫₀^{vᵢ} p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ)dx) yields the seller the largest possible expected revenue.
items.proof_sketch: By Claim_9.4.3_c, the mechanism achieves the revenue upper bound (9.14). By Claim_9.4.3_f, under (9.18), constraint (i) is satisfied. Constraints (ii) and (iii) hold by construction.

items.statement: The marginal revenue from bidder i at value vᵢ is MRᵢ(vᵢ) = vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ). This represents the marginal revenue the seller obtains from increasing the probability that the object is assigned to bidder i when his value is vᵢ.
items.context: The virtual valuation vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is interpreted as marginal revenue.

notation_in_scope.MRᵢ(vᵢ): marginal revenue from bidder i at value vᵢ

items.statement: The marginal revenue interpretation: increasing the probability that the object is awarded to bidder i with value vᵢ increases revenue at rate vᵢfᵢ(vᵢ) (from charging bidder i more) but decreases revenue by 1-Fᵢ(vᵢ) (from incentive compatibility requiring reduced costs for all higher values v'ᵢ > vᵢ). The net marginal revenue per unit density is therefore MRᵢ(vᵢ) = vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ).
items.proof_sketch: The density of vᵢ is fᵢ(vᵢ), so revenue increases at rate vᵢfᵢ(vᵢ). By constraint (ii), increasing probability for lower values reduces one-for-one the cost for higher values; mass 1-Fᵢ(vᵢ) above vᵢ gives total reduction 1-Fᵢ(vᵢ). Net total effect: vᵢfᵢ(vᵢ) - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ)), so per-density marginal revenue is vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ).
items.context: Intuitive derivation of why the virtual valuation equals marginal revenue.

items.statement: The allocation rule assigns probability one to the bidder with highest MRᵢ(vᵢ), so long as it is positive. If all marginal revenues are negative, the seller keeps the object. This is revenue-maximizing because if MRᵢ(vᵢ) > MRⱼ(vⱼ), the seller increases revenue by shifting probability from bidder j to bidder i.
items.proof_sketch: Direct consequence of the marginal revenue interpretation.
items.context: Interpretation of the optimal allocation rule from (9.16) in terms of marginal revenue.

items.statement: In the optimal mechanism, if bidder i does not receive the object (p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 0), then c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 0, i.e., bidder i pays nothing.
items.proof: By (9.17), c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ)vᵢ - ∫₀^{vᵢ} p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ)dx = 0·vᵢ - ∫₀^{vᵢ} p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ)dx. By assumption (9.18), p*_i(·,v₋ᵢ) is non-decreasing. Since p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 0, it follows that p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ) = 0 for every x ≤ vᵢ. Hence the integral is zero, so c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 0.
items.context: First part of simplifying the payment rule of the optimal mechanism.

items.statement: Define r*_i(v₋ᵢ) as the largest value for bidder i such that p*_i(r*_i,v₋ᵢ) = 0. That is, r*_i(v₋ᵢ) is the threshold value below which bidder i does not receive the object, given the other bidders' values v₋ᵢ.
items.context: r*_i is defined when p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1, and represents the critical value separating winning from losing.

notation_in_scope.r*_i(v₋ᵢ): largest value for bidder i at which he does not receive the object

items.statement: In the optimal mechanism, if bidder i receives the object (p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1), then c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = r*_i(v₋ᵢ). That is, the winning bidder pays a price equal to the maximum value he could have reported without receiving the object, and this price is independent of his own reported value.
items.proof: When p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1, by (9.17): c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = vᵢ - ∫₀^{vᵢ} p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ)dx. Since p*_i takes values 0 or 1, is non-decreasing and continuous from the left, and p*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = 1, there exists r*_i < vᵢ such that p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ) = 1 for x > r*_i(v₋ᵢ) and p*_i(x,v₋ᵢ) = 0 for x ≤ r*_i(v₋ᵢ). Therefore c*_i(vᵢ,v₋ᵢ) = vᵢ - ∫_{r*_i(v₋ᵢ)}^{vᵢ} 1dx = vᵢ - (vᵢ - r*_i(v₋ᵢ)) = r*_i(v₋ᵢ).
items.context: Second part of simplifying the payment rule: winners pay a price independent of their own value.

items.statement: If N bidders have independent private values with bidder i's value drawn from the continuous positive density fᵢ and each vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is strictly increasing, then the following direct selling mechanism yields the seller the largest possible expected revenue: For each reported vector of values v₁,...,vₙ, the seller assigns the object to the bidder i whose vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) is strictly largest and positive. If there is no such bidder, the seller keeps the object and no payments are made. If there is such a bidder i, then only this bidder makes a payment to the seller in the amount r*_i, where r*_i - (1-Fᵢ(r*_i))/fᵢ(r*_i) = 0 or maxⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ - (1-Fⱼ(vⱼ))/fⱼ(vⱼ), whichever is largest. Bidder i's payment r*_i is the largest value he could have reported, given the others' reported values, without receiving the object.
items.proof_sketch: Follows from Theorem 9.7 combined with Claims 9.4.4_c and 9.4.4_d which simplify the payment rule.

notation_in_scope.r*_i: payment amount = largest value bidder i could report without winning

items.statement: In the optimal selling mechanism defined by Theorem 9.8, truth-telling is a dominant strategy for each bidder, not merely a Nash equilibrium. Even if other bidders do not report truthfully, bidder i can do no better than to report his value truthfully.
items.context: Stated as a fact that the reader is asked to show in the exercises.

items.statement: One drawback of the optimal selling mechanism is that to implement it, the seller must know the distributions Fᵢ from which the bidders' values are drawn. This is in contrast to the four standard auctions that the seller can implement without any bidder information whatsoever.
items.context: Observation about practical limitations of the optimal mechanism.

items.statement: In the optimal selling mechanism, the object is not always allocated efficiently. There are two sources of inefficiency: (1) The seller sometimes keeps the object even though his value for it is zero and all bidders have positive values, which occurs when every bidder i's value vᵢ satisfies vᵢ - (1-Fᵢ(vᵢ))/fᵢ(vᵢ) ≤ 0. (2) Even when the seller assigns the object, it might not go to the bidder with the highest value, which can occur when bidders are asymmetric (Fᵢ ≠ Fⱼ).
items.proof_sketch: For (2): if bidders are asymmetric, for some v ∈ [0,1], v - (1-F₁(v))/f₁(v) > v - (1-F₂(v))/f₂(v) > 0. When both bidders' values are v, bidder 1 wins. By continuity, if bidder 1's value falls slightly to v' < v, the inequality v' - (1-F₁(v'))/f₁(v') > v - (1-F₂(v))/f₂(v) continues to hold, so bidder 1 wins despite having lower value.
items.context: Analysis of allocative efficiency in the optimal mechanism. The seller acts as a monopolist restricting supply.

items.statement: Under symmetry (fᵢ = f and Fᵢ = F for all i), if v - (1-F(v))/f(v) is strictly increasing, the optimal selling mechanism assigns the object to the bidder with the strictly highest value vᵢ, provided vᵢ > ρ* where ρ* ∈ [0,1] satisfies ρ* - (1-F(ρ*))/f(ρ*) = 0. The winner pays the larger of ρ* and the largest value reported by the other bidders.
items.proof_sketch: Because v - (1-F(v))/f(v) is strictly increasing and F is the same for all bidders, the bidder with highest vᵢ also has the highest virtual valuation. The threshold for receiving the object is that the virtual valuation be positive, which is equivalent to vᵢ > ρ*.
items.context: Simplification of the optimal mechanism under the assumption of symmetric bidders.

items.statement: The optimal reserve price ρ* ∈ [0,1] is defined as the unique solution to ρ* - (1-F(ρ*))/f(ρ*) = 0, where F is the common CDF and f is the common PDF of bidders' values under symmetry.
items.context: This is equation (9.19). The existence and uniqueness of ρ* is left as an exercise.

items.statement: Under symmetry, the optimal direct selling mechanism can be mimicked by running a second-price auction with reserve price ρ*: the bidder with the highest bid strictly above ρ* wins and pays the second-highest bid or ρ*, whichever is larger. If no bids exceed ρ*, the seller keeps the object. This is optimal because it is a dominant strategy to bid one's value in a second-price auction with a reserve price.
items.proof_sketch: In the symmetric optimal mechanism, the winner pays max(ρ*, max_{j≠i} vⱼ), which is exactly what happens in a second-price auction with reserve price ρ*. Dominant strategy truthfulness follows from the standard second-price auction argument extended to include a reserve price.
items.context: Establishes the connection between the optimal mechanism and a second-price auction with reserve price.

items.statement: If N bidders have independent private values, each drawn from the same continuous positive density f, where v - (1-F(v))/f(v) is strictly increasing, then a second-price auction with reserve price ρ* satisfying ρ* - (1-F(ρ*))/f(ρ*) = 0 maximises the seller's expected revenue.
items.proof_sketch: Under symmetry the optimal mechanism reduces to assigning the object to the highest bidder above ρ* and charging max(ρ*, second-highest value), which is exactly a second-price auction with reserve price ρ*.

items.statement: Adding an appropriate reserve price to each of the four standard auctions (first-price, second-price, Dutch, English) renders each of them optimal for the seller under symmetry.
items.context: The four standard auctions yield the same revenue under symmetry (revenue equivalence), and each can be made optimal by adding a reserve price.

items.statement: Let X denote the finite set of social states. There are N individuals in society. For each individual i, let Tᵢ denote the finite set of possible types. There is a common prior q, where q(t) > 0 is the probability that the vector of types is t = (t₁,...,tₙ) ∈ T = ×ᵢ₌₁ᴺ Tᵢ. The types are independent: q(t) = q₁(t₁)···qₙ(tₙ).
items.context: Setup of the general mechanism design framework for allocative efficiency.

notation_in_scope.Tᵢ: finite set of types of individual i

items.statement: Quasi-linear utility: If individual i has m dollars and x ∈ X is the social state, his von Neumann-Morgenstern utility is vᵢ(x,tᵢ) + m when his type is tᵢ ∈ Tᵢ. Here vᵢ(x,tᵢ) is the value, in dollars, that individual i places on social state x when his type is tᵢ. Individual i's value depends only on his own type tᵢ (private values).
items.context: Restriction to quasi-linear preferences with private values for the remainder of the chapter.

notation_in_scope.vᵢ(x,tᵢ): individual i's value for social state x given type tᵢ

items.statement: Consider a small town with N individuals choosing between a swimming pool (S) or a bridge (B), so X = {S,B}. Each individual i has quasi-linear preferences with private type tᵢ, equally likely to take values 1,2,...,9, with types independent across individuals. Individual i's values are: vᵢ(S,tᵢ) = tᵢ + 5, vᵢ(B,tᵢ) = 2tᵢ. Individual i strictly prefers S when tᵢ ∈ {1,2,3,4}, strictly prefers B when tᵢ ∈ {6,7,8,9}, and is indifferent when tᵢ = 5.

With quasi-linear preferences (no private information), a social state x̂ ∈ X is Pareto efficient if and only if it maximises the sum of the non-monetary parts of individual utilities, i.e., if and only if x̂ solves max_{x∈X} Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ vᵢ(x).
items.context: This is the claim stated in (9.20). A key characterization of Pareto efficiency under quasi-linearity.

notation_in_scope.vᵢ(x): individual i's non-monetary utility from social state x

items.statement: ('Only if' direction of (9.20)) If y ∈ X satisfies Σᵢ vᵢ(y) > Σᵢ vᵢ(x), then x is not Pareto efficient. Specifically, switching from x to y combined with income transfers τᵢ = vᵢ(x) - vᵢ(y) + (1/N)Σⱼ(vⱼ(y) - vⱼ(x)) yields a strict Pareto improvement: the τᵢ sum to zero, and each individual's utility change vᵢ(y) + τᵢ - vᵢ(x) = (1/N)Σⱼ(vⱼ(y) - vⱼ(x)) > 0.
items.proof: Suppose y satisfies Σᵢ vᵢ(y) > Σᵢ vᵢ(x). Define transfers τᵢ = vᵢ(x) - vᵢ(y) + (1/N)Σⱼ(vⱼ(y) - vⱼ(x)). By construction, Σᵢ τᵢ = 0. After changing state from x to y with these transfers, the change in individual i's utility is vᵢ(y) + τᵢ - vᵢ(x) = (1/N)Σⱼ(vⱼ(y) - vⱼ(x)), which by assumption (9.21) is strictly positive. Hence each individual is strictly better off, so x is not Pareto efficient.
items.context: Proves that a social state not maximizing the sum of utilities is not Pareto efficient. The 'if' part is left as Exercise 9.26.

items.statement: An allocation function is a function x: T → X that specifies, for each vector of individual types, a social state in X.
items.context: Because individual preferences depend on types, achieving efficiency typically requires the social state to depend on types.

items.statement: An allocation function x̂: T → X is ex post Pareto-efficient if for each t ∈ T, x̂(t) ∈ X solves max_{x∈X} Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ vᵢ(x,tᵢ), where the maximisation is over all social states. We then say that x̂(t) is an ex post efficient social state given t ∈ T.

notation_in_scope.vᵢ(x,tᵢ): individual i's value for state x given type tᵢ

items.statement: In general, ex ante Pareto efficiency implies interim Pareto efficiency implies ex post Pareto efficiency. The greater the uncertainty, the greater the scope for mutually beneficial insurance.
items.context: Hierarchy of efficiency concepts at different stages: ex ante (before types known), interim (own type known), ex post (all types known).

items.statement: A direct mechanism consists of a collection of probability assignment functions p_x(t₁,...,tₙ), one for each x ∈ X, and N cost functions c₁(t₁,...,tₙ),...,cₙ(t₁,...,tₙ). For every reported type vector (t₁,...,tₙ) ∈ T, p_x(t₁,...,tₙ) ∈ [0,1] denotes the probability that the social state is x ∈ X and cᵢ(t₁,...,tₙ) ∈ ℝ denotes individual i's cost (amount paid). The constraint Σ_{x∈X} p_x(t₁,...,tₙ) = 1 must hold for every (t₁,...,tₙ) ∈ T.

notation_in_scope.p_x: probability assignment for social state x

items.statement: Definition 9.4 becomes equivalent to Definition 9.1 (direct selling mechanism for a single object) when (i) there is a single object available, (ii) there are N+1 individuals consisting of N bidders and one seller, and (iii) the social states are the N+1 allocations in which either one of the bidders ends up with the good or the seller ends up with the good.
items.context: Connection between the general direct mechanism framework and the single-object auction setting.

items.statement: Given a direct mechanism, define uᵢ(rᵢ,tᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ∈T₋ᵢ} q₋ᵢ(t₋ᵢ)[Σ_{x∈X} p_x(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ)vᵢ(x,tᵢ) - cᵢ(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ)] as individual i's expected utility from reporting type rᵢ when his true type is tᵢ and all others report truthfully. Also define p̄ᵢˣ(rᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ} q₋ᵢ(t₋ᵢ)p_x(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ) and c̄ᵢ(rᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ} q₋ᵢ(t₋ᵢ)cᵢ(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ), so that uᵢ(rᵢ,tᵢ) = Σ_{x∈X} p̄ᵢˣ(rᵢ)vᵢ(x,tᵢ) - c̄ᵢ(rᵢ).
items.context: Expected utility notation for the general mechanism design framework. Equations (9.22) and (9.23).

notation_in_scope.uᵢ(rᵢ,tᵢ): individual i's expected utility from reporting rᵢ when true type is tᵢ
notation_in_scope.p̄ᵢˣ(rᵢ): expected probability of state x when i reports rᵢ
notation_in_scope.c̄ᵢ(rᵢ): expected cost when i reports rᵢ

items.statement: A direct mechanism is incentive-compatible if when the other individuals always report their types truthfully, each individual's expected utility is maximised by always reporting his type truthfully. That is, the mechanism is incentive-compatible if for each individual i and for each tᵢ ∈ Tᵢ, uᵢ(rᵢ,tᵢ) as defined in (9.23) is maximised in rᵢ ∈ Tᵢ when rᵢ = tᵢ. Equivalently, the mechanism is incentive-compatible if it is a Bayesian-Nash equilibrium for each individual to always report his type truthfully.

The revelation principle applies to the general mechanism design setting: if any extensive form game (mechanism) has a Bayesian-Nash equilibrium in which an ex post efficient social state always occurs, then there exists an incentive-compatible direct mechanism that achieves the same ex post efficient outcome. The direct mechanism simply plays the individuals' equilibrium strategies for them after they report their types.
items.proof_sketch: Design a direct mechanism that plays equilibrium strategies on behalf of individuals. If others report honestly, it is as if you participate in the original game against them. Since it was optimal to play the equilibrium strategy conditional on your actual type, it is optimal to report your type truthfully so those actions are carried out on your behalf.
items.context: Informal statement of the revelation principle for the general quasi-linear setting.

items.statement: An incentive-compatible direct mechanism is ex post efficient if it assigns probability one to a set of ex post efficient social states given any vector of reported types t ∈ T, i.e., if for every t ∈ T, p_x(t) > 0 implies x ∈ X is ex post efficient when the vector of types is t.
items.context: Terminology for incentive-compatible mechanisms that achieve ex post efficiency.

items.statement: Let x̂: T → X be an ex post efficient allocation function, i.e., for each t ∈ T, x̂(t) solves max_{x∈X} Σⱼ₌₁ᴺ vⱼ(x,tⱼ). For each individual i, let x̃ᵢ: T₋ᵢ → X be an ex post efficient allocation function in the society without individual i, i.e., for each t₋ᵢ ∈ T₋ᵢ, x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) solves max_{x∈X} Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x,tⱼ).
items.context: Setup for defining externalities in the VCG mechanism. x̂ and x̃ᵢ remain fixed for the rest of the chapter.

notation_in_scope.x̂(t): ex post efficient allocation with all individuals
notation_in_scope.x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ): ex post efficient allocation without individual i

items.statement: The externality imposed by individual i when the type vector is t ∈ T is the difference in the total utility of the others when i is not present versus when he is present: Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ). This externality is always non-negative.
items.proof_sketch: Non-negativity follows because x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) maximises Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x,tⱼ) by definition.
items.context: The externality measures the cost individual i imposes on others by his presence.

items.statement: In the case of a single good, each individual's externality is zero except for the individual with the highest value, whose externality equals the second-highest value.
items.proof_sketch: If the winner were not present, the bidder with second-highest value would have won. The externality is the difference in others' utility, which equals the second-highest value minus zero.
items.context: Verifies that the externality concept reduces to the second-price auction payment in the single-good case.

items.statement: The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) Mechanism: Each individual simultaneously reports his type to the designer. If the reported vector of types is t ∈ T, the social state x̂(t) is chosen. In addition, each individual i is assessed a monetary cost equal to cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) = Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ). That is, each individual pays his externality based on the reported types.

Continuing Example 9.3, the ex post efficient allocation function is: x̂(t) = B if Σᵢ(tᵢ - 5) > 0, and x̂(t) = S otherwise. Individual i is pivotal for B at t if Σⱼ(tⱼ - 5) > 0 and Σⱼ≠ᵢ(tⱼ - 5) ≤ 0. Individual i is pivotal for S at t if Σⱼ(tⱼ - 5) ≤ 0 and Σⱼ≠ᵢ(tⱼ - 5) > 0. The VCG cost is: cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) = Σⱼ≠ᵢ(5 - tⱼ) if i is pivotal for B, Σⱼ≠ᵢ(tⱼ - 5) if i is pivotal for S, and 0 otherwise.
items.proof_sketch: When i is pivotal for B: without i the state would be S, others' utility from S is Σⱼ≠ᵢ(tⱼ + 5), and from B (with i) is Σⱼ≠ᵢ 2tⱼ. Externality = Σⱼ≠ᵢ(tⱼ + 5) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ 2tⱼ = Σⱼ≠ᵢ(5 - tⱼ).

items.statement: In the VCG mechanism it is a weakly dominant strategy for each individual to report his type truthfully. Hence, the VCG mechanism is incentive-compatible and ex post efficient.
items.proof: We show truthful reporting is weakly dominant for arbitrary individual i. Suppose others report t₋ᵢ ∈ T₋ᵢ (not necessarily truthfully), i's type is tᵢ, and he reports rᵢ. His utility is vᵢ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tᵢ) - cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ). Substituting the VCG cost definition: vᵢ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tᵢ) - [Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tⱼ)] = Σⱼ₌₁ᴺ vⱼ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ). (P.2) We need rᵢ = tᵢ to maximise this. Since rᵢ appears only in the first sum, it suffices to show Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(tᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) ≥ Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) for all rᵢ. This holds because x̂(tᵢ,t₋ᵢ) maximises Σⱼ vⱼ(x,tⱼ) over all x ∈ X by definition, and x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ) ∈ X.

items.statement: Each individual's VCG cost cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) is always non-negative, so the VCG mechanism never runs a deficit and typically runs a surplus.
items.proof_sketch: By definition, cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) = Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ) ≥ 0 because x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) maximises Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x,tⱼ).
items.context: Important property of VCG costs that motivates the search for budget-balanced mechanisms.

items.statement: It is an equilibrium for all N individuals to voluntarily participate in the VCG mechanism. If individual i participates and reports truthfully, his payoff when the type vector is t is vᵢ(x̂(t),tᵢ) - cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) = Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ). If he does not participate, the social state becomes x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) and his utility is vᵢ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tᵢ). Participation is weakly preferred because Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ) ≥ Σⱼ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) by definition of x̂(t).
items.proof: By definition of x̂(t), Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ) ≥ Σⱼ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) because x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) ∈ X. Rearranging: Σⱼ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) ≥ vᵢ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tᵢ). Hence, by (9.24), i's utility from participating exceeds (9.25), his utility from not participating.
items.context: Voluntary participation result for the VCG mechanism.

items.statement: The dominance of truth-telling in the VCG mechanism does not contradict the Gibbard-Satterthwaite Theorem (Theorem 6.4) because preferences are restricted to the quasi-linear domain. The function x̂(·) is strategy-proof and may be non-dictatorial, but this is consistent because the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem requires unrestricted preferences.
items.proof_sketch: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem assumes an unrestricted domain of preferences. Here preferences are restricted to quasi-linear form, which permits strategy-proof non-dictatorial social choice functions.
items.context: Reconciliation with the impossibility result from Chapter 6.

items.statement: If the VCG surplus revenue is destroyed, the overall outcome (social state plus money) is not ex post Pareto efficient. If redistributed to the N individuals, the costs cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(t) overstate actual costs and it is no longer clear that truth-telling remains dominant once individuals account for their share of redistributed revenue.
items.context: Motivation for seeking budget-balanced mechanisms: the VCG surplus creates problems whether destroyed or redistributed.

items.statement: The cost functions c₁,...,cₙ are budget-balanced if they sum to zero regardless of the reported vector of types, i.e., if Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ cᵢ(t) = 0 for every t ∈ T. If a direct mechanism's cost functions are budget-balanced then the mechanism is budget-balanced as well.

The expected externality of individual i when his type is tᵢ is c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ∈T₋ᵢ} q₋ᵢ(t₋ᵢ) cᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ,t₋ᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ∈T₋ᵢ} q₋ᵢ(t₋ᵢ)[Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̃ᵢ(t₋ᵢ),tⱼ) - Σⱼ≠ᵢ vⱼ(x̂(t),tⱼ)]. This is individual i's VCG cost averaged over other individuals' types.
items.context: Equation (9.26). These expected externalities are used to construct the budget-balanced mechanism.

notation_in_scope.c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ): expected externality of individual i given type tᵢ

items.statement: Consider the mechanism in which, when the vector of reported types is t ∈ T, the ex post efficient social state x̂(t) is chosen and individual i's cost is c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ) - c̄ᵢ₊₁ᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ₊₁), where i+1 = 1 when i = N. This budget-balanced expected externality mechanism is incentive-compatible, ex post efficient, and budget-balanced. Furthermore, in the truth-telling equilibrium, every individual is voluntarily willing to participate regardless of his type.
items.proof: Budget-balance is immediate since the costs telescope around the circular arrangement, summing to zero. For incentive compatibility: let uᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ,tᵢ) denote i's expected utility in the VCG mechanism when reporting rᵢ with true type tᵢ. Then uᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ,tᵢ) = Σ_{t₋ᵢ} q(t₋ᵢ)vᵢ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tᵢ) - c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ), which is maximised at rᵢ = tᵢ (truth-telling is dominant in VCG). In the new mechanism, i's expected costs are c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ) - Σ_{tᵢ₊₁} qᵢ₊₁(tᵢ₊₁)c̄ᵢ₊₁ᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ₊₁). Hence expected utility is Σ_{t₋ᵢ} q(t₋ᵢ)vᵢ(x̂(rᵢ,t₋ᵢ),tᵢ) - c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ) + c̄ᵢ₊₁ = uᵢᵛᶜᴳ(rᵢ,tᵢ) + c̄ᵢ₊₁, where c̄ᵢ₊₁ is a constant. Since uᵢᵛᶜᴳ is maximised at rᵢ = tᵢ, so is this expression. For voluntary participation: c̄ᵢ₊₁ ≥ 0 (it equals i+1's ex ante expected VCG cost), so i is at least as well off as in the VCG mechanism. Since participation is individually rational in VCG, it is also rational here.

items.statement: Theorem 9.11 does NOT establish that truth-telling is a weakly dominant strategy in the budget-balanced expected externality mechanism. It only establishes that truth-telling is a Bayesian-Nash equilibrium. Thus, gaining budget balance (and hence full efficiency) comes at the cost of losing the dominant strategy property.
items.context: Important caveat. Green and Laffont (1977) and Holmstrom (1979b) show it is impossible to achieve both budget balance and dominant strategy incentive compatibility in a wide variety of circumstances.

items.statement: Continuing Examples 9.3 and 9.4 with N = 2 individuals, the budget-balanced expected externality mechanism yields the following cost table. If individual reports type tᵢ ∈ {1,2,...,9}, he pays the other individual c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ) as follows: type 1 → 10/9, type 2 → 2/3, type 3 → 1/3, type 4 → 1/9, type 5 → 0, type 6 → 1/9, type 7 → 1/3, type 8 → 2/3, type 9 → 10/9. The bridge is built if the sum of reports exceeds 10, the swimming pool otherwise. This mechanism is incentive-compatible, ex post efficient, budget-balanced, and leads to voluntary participation.
items.proof_sketch: The entries are the expected VCG costs c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ). For example, c̄₁ᵛᶜᴳ(4) = (1/9)(6-5) = 1/9 because individual 1 is pivotal for S only when t₂ = 6, which happens with probability 1/9, and his VCG cost is 6-5 = 1.

notation_in_scope.c̄ᵢᵛᶜᴳ(tᵢ): expected VCG cost = payment to the other individual

items.statement: For each individual i and for each tᵢ ∈ Tᵢ, let IRᵢ(tᵢ) denote i's expected utility when he does not participate in the mechanism and his type is tᵢ. This captures property rights over social states: the value of non-participation depends on what social states are available without individual i.
items.context: Generalizes the participation constraint to allow type-dependent outside options. For a seller with value vₛ for an object, IR₁(vₛ) = vₛ; for a buyer, IR₂(vᵦ) = 0.

notation_in_scope.IRᵢ(tᵢ): individual i's outside option utility given type tᵢ

items.statement: An incentive-compatible direct mechanism is individually rational if for each individual i and for each tᵢ ∈ Tᵢ, i's expected utility from participating in the mechanism and reporting truthfully when his type is tᵢ is at least IRᵢ(tᵢ) when the others participate and always report their types truthfully.

notation_in_scope.IRᵢ(tᵢ): individual i's outside option utility given type tᵢ

items.statement: The earlier analysis implicitly assumed that individuals cannot be forced to give up their income (no lump-sum taxation) and that they have no property rights over social states (non-participation does not affect the set of available social states). These assumptions are sometimes inappropriate, e.g., when the seller is included as a participant in an auction, or in partnership dissolution problems.
items.context: Motivation for introducing type-dependent individual rationality constraints and property rights.
